item.title: Stock markets mount a huge comeback
item.description:
On Monday, Morgan Stanley's Mike Wilson recommended a maximum overweight on global equities, saying the AI capex cycle remains in tact.

Earlier today, that looked like folly but now it looks like a gutsy call that could be remembered for years.

"This is the fat pitch we have patiently been waiting for, and we're not going to miss it," Wilson's team wrote in a note Monday. "Markets bottom on bad news and deleveraging. We have had a lot of both."

Earlier today, the Fear & Greed index hit 9 in a sign that negative sentiment was overdone.

In terms of the internals, Anthropic and Meta were among the first to turn. That suggests that some of the post-IPO sentiment around ANT may be washed out. It hit a low of $73.85 just after the open before a rapid turn.

The moves are snowballing elsewhere with broad gains, including a 9% rally from the bottom in Micron (which is still the worst S&P 500 performer on the day).

The chipmakers have all gained but remain red. Meanwhile, the advancers lead decliners by 4:1. 

At last check, the S&P 500 was down 0.2% and the Nasdaq Composite down 0.8%. If we can finish here (or green) it will be a big lift for the bulls into Thanksgiving. I wonder if this is a short-covering rally in a holiday-shortened week but -- at worst -- it's a sign of life.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Baker Hughes US rig count holds steady at 607. Oil rigs rise by one.
item.description:
Baker Hughes reported that the US rotary rig count was unchanged at 607 in its November 25 report. The addition of one oil rig offset a decline of one natural gas rig.

  • Oil rigs 470 vs 469 last week, up 1. Up 63 from a year ago.
  • Natural gas rigs 127 vs 128 last week, down 1. Down 3 from a year ago.
  • Miscellaneous rigs 10 vs 10 last week, unchanged. Up 3 from a year ago.
  • Total US rigs 607 vs 607 last week, unchanged. Up 63 from a year ago.

The US land rig count rose by one to 592, while the offshore count fell by one to 14. The Gulf of Mexico accounted for that decline, slipping to 13 rigs from 14.

The bigger move is in the year-over-year numbers. The US is running 63 more rigs than it did a year ago, and oil rigs account for the entire net increase.

Crude oil is trading up $1.62 at $83.67 the price.. The prices just below the high for the day at $83.85. That will also is near a swing area at $83.88 (low from November 10 and highs from November 19 and November 20).  Move above and the falling 100 hour moving average at $86.55 would be targeted.

With the stock market fragile and with tariff anxiety along with AI and chip concern, the Trump administration does not need to see oil prices moving back to the upside.  

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump blames the election for the selloff. Here’s what I’m watching.
item.description:
President Trump blamed the November 3 election results for the drop in stocks in a Wednesday post on Truth Social.

The first place I’d look is the chip stocks. The Nasdaq was down about 4% in morning trading versus roughly 2.5% for the S&P 500. Nvidia was down nearly 9% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index was off more than 7%. The bounce on Jensen Huang’s return on Monday - orchestrated by the WHite House - gave buyers an opening, and sellers came right back in. The election added to concerns about tighter AI regulation, but with the Jensen Huang allegations, and reinstatement, who can blame the need for more regulation - not the wild, wild west with unlimited uncertainty.  When trust goes out the window and we live on the edge of under-regulation, that is a problem. Then there’s a bigger question for these stocks at current valuations. How much profit will all that AI spending generate, and how long will investors have to wait for it?

The war with Iran is another reason buyers are hesitant despite the recent fall in the price of oil. Iran said two tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. As long as safe passage is in doubt, so is the outlook for oil supplies. Another jump in fuel prices would leave consumers with less to spend and squeeze profit margins. Looking at the price of oil, although it is well off the highs near $120, the price at $83.50 is still well off the levels on February 27 - the Friday before the start of the war. That level was at $67.30.  The closing price at the end of 2025 was at $57.40.  If $80 is the low, that is still feeding inflation.  Add in fresh tariff proposals from Washington.  Why does Pres Trump and company think tariffs are what Americans want especially in times of inflation where corporations are already fighting higher costs.  Core PCE inflation rose  to 3.3% from 3.1%, and a December Fed hike stays in play. 

Then there’s the trust issue in Washington. Can businesses count on the policies they’re making plans around? If you don’t know what your import costs will be in six months, it’s harder to commit to hiring or investment. And if investors have less confidence in what companies will earn, they’ll pay less for those earnings.

Nevertheless, for me, the chip stocks are still the near-term barometer. If it weren't for the AI revolution where would we be.  As a result, with stocks at recent lows, that is a concern. Morever, the bounce that we saw on Monday was just into resistance which stalled the rally and led to an equally as fast decline back to the lows on Friday.  

The Pres. Trump attempt to push higher was met with a resounding vote of no-confidence.   

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: European stocks close lower as the Nasdaq 100 sheds nearly 4%.
item.description:
As London and European traders head home for the day, the major indices are all lower. Spain’s Ibex led the declines with a -2.00% drop, followed by Italy’s FTSE MIB at -1.81%. The UK’s FTSE 100 held up the best of the group, closing down -0.38%.

Monday’s rally on Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO is looking more and more like a relief rally. The gains started to unwind on Tuesday, and today the sellers are getting follow-through. Fresh tariff proposals following the U.S. investigation into excess industrial capacity give traders another reason to cut exposure. For the Fed, the timing is awkward. Core inflation is already running at 3.3% year over year, and higher tariffs could make it harder to bring that number down if companies pass the costs along.  Washington seems to sit on the edge of scorching the earth, but then throw the "Big News" (like Jensen Huang intervention), that allows for the "grifting" to fill the coffers.  

The European closes.  Major indices all fall

  • German DAX fell 284.61 points, or -1.14%, to 24,733.21.
  • France’s CAC 40 fell 59.93 points, or -0.75%, to 7,980.57.
  • UK FTSE 100 fell 40.13 points, or -0.38%, to 10,426.95.
  • Spain’s Ibex 35 fell 380.01 points, or -2.00%, to 18,635.80.
  • Italy’s FTSE MIB fell 872.04 points, or -1.81%, to 47,249.14.

European bond yields move lower.

German and UK 10-year yields led the move lower, both falling nearly 6 basis points. Italy’s 10-year yield edged down just 0.6 basis points, widening its spread over Germany by 5.3 basis points even as yields fell across the board.

  • Germany 3.222%, down -5.9 basis points.
  • France 4.737%, down -4.8 basis points.
  • UK 5.136%, down -5.8 basis points.
  • Spain 3.849%, down -3.5 basis points.
  • Italy 4.358%, down -0.6 basis points.

U.S. stocks. The selling is still heaviest in chips and AI.

As Europe closes, the Nasdaq 100 is down more than 1,000 points. SanDisk is down -12.66%, Micron is down -12.23% and Lam Research is down -11.68%. AMD and Marvell are each down about -9%. The Dow and Russell 2000 are also lower, but the gap between those indices and the Nasdaq tells you where the selling is concentrated.

  • Dow down 628.06 points, or -1.26%, at 49,395.93.
  • S&P 500 down 179.99 points, or -2.50%, at 7,021.10.
  • Nasdaq Composite down 875.77 points, or -3.69%, at 22,857.76.
  • Russell 2000 down 39.74 points, or -1.48%, at 2,645.20.
  • Nasdaq 100 down 1,045.54 points, or -3.99%, at 25,168.62.

U.S. data. Stronger growth and firmer annual core inflation.

Third-quarter GDP was revised up to 4.3% annualized from 3.4%, well above the 3.5% estimate. Consumer spending was stronger than first reported, rising at a 4.2% pace versus 3.8% in the advance estimate. Weekly initial jobless claims fell 13,000 to 189,000 from a revised 202,000, while continuing claims dropped 95,000 to 1.697 million. October new home sales rose to a 701,000 annualized pace versus 650,000 expected, although September was revised down to 614,000 from 676,000. bea.gov

On prices, October core PCE rose 0.3% on the month, as expected. The annual rate was the part that stood out. It rose to 3.3% from 3.1%, above the 3.2% estimate. Headline PCE rose to 3.8% year over year from 3.6%. Personal income rose a stronger-than-expected 0.7%, while spending rose 0.3% and was flat after adjusting for inflation. For the Fed, the combination of stronger third-quarter growth, low claims and firmer annual core inflation leaves little urgency to ease. investinglive.com

Gold and bitcoin trade lower with stocks. Oil moves higher.

Spot gold is down 2.79% near $3,457, and silver is taking a bigger hit, down 5.38% near $38.71. The move in gold stands out because yields are lower. When stocks and metals are both getting hit and bonds are catching a bid, the price action is consistent with traders raising cash across positions. For gold, the next level I’m watching is $3,425. That’s the barometer for whether buyers can slow the decline.

Bitcoin is down 2.34% near $58,344 after trading below the $57,735–$58,035 swing area earlier in the session. It’s back above that area at the European close. Can the buyers hold it on a retest? A move back below would put the earlier low near $57,209 back in play, followed by the weekend low at $55,081.

WTI crude is up 1.39% at $83.19. Copper is down 2.10% at $5.2560

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: US treasury sells $44 billion of 7-year notes at a high yield of 4.708%
item.description:
The US treasury sold 44 billion of 70 or notes:

  • WI level at the time of the auction: 4.698%
  • High yield: 4.708%
  • WI level at the time of the auction: 4.698%
  • Tail: 1.0 basis point vs the average of 0.1 basis point
  • Bid to cover: 2.43X vs the average of 2.48X
  • Directs: 33.19% vs the average of 24.64%
  • Indirects: 58.20% vs the average of 63.64%
  • Dealers: 8.61% vs the average of 11.72%

Auction grade: C+

The auction was mixed but still better than average. The high yield came in 1.0 basis point above the when-issued level, and the bid to cover was a touch below average. Indirect bidders took a smaller share than usual, but stronger direct demand more than made up for that shortfall, leaving dealers with just 8.61% of the issue. The lighter dealer takedown was a positive that tipped the grade to above average but still on the border between a C+ and a B-.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: We are in the railway boom, but just discovered the airplane
item.description:
Imagine it's 1870 and you're investing in railways. The world is on the cusp of an enormous increase in demand for transportation. You buy land, lay tracks, build stations and invest in steel production.

Then someone invents the airplane.

I increasingly wonder if that's what's happening in AI.

The breakthroughs in mathematics over the past few days are remarkable in their own right. They are the clearest evidence that super intelligence isn't Anthropic IPO hype. They point to broad, rapid advances.

Further, a published look inside Anthropic shows there is no ceiling on AI.

Moreover, it looks like we're are now turning the intellectual firepower of AI back on AI itself.

People talk about the killer app of AI being discovering drugs or limitless power and that's true in the bigger picture. In the smaller picture though, there is $9 trillion being spent on AI infrastructure right now and the most-valuable investment in the next 10 quarters is a way to dramatically lower those costs, while still racing towards frontier AI.

The bottlenecks right now are compute, compute infrastructure and power.

If AI can solve decades-old mathematical problems and discover entirely new computational frameworks, why wouldn't it be able to discover radically more efficient ways of producing intelligence?

In fact, that will be among its first tasks. There is no higher-return research project for an AI company than making AI itself more intelligent and more efficient. Every success makes the next discovery cheaper and easier. It can eliminate its own bottlenecks.

That's recursive self-improvement and it introduces a dynamic that has no real historical parallel. The steam engine couldn't invent a better steam engine.

There is an implicit contradiction in the AI investment narrative right now. On the one hand, we're told that AI will revolutionize medicine, engineering, manufacturing and virtually every other field of human endeavour. On the other hand, we're making enormous, decades-long infrastructure investments based on something resembling a linear trajectory of AI computing requirements.

Why would AI revolutionize everything except itself?

The transformer architecture was invented in 2017, ChatGPT 3 in 2022. The history of humanity's efforts to create artificial intelligence is remarkably short. The idea that we're anywhere near the optimal mathematical architecture for intelligence is unlikely.

Perhaps we're doing the computational equivalent of trying to multiply large numbers using Roman numerals. 

Given some of the leaks coming out of the labs, I think that's what is happening and why markets are freaking out about chips, data centers and power investment. We won't need it, or at least not at the pace it's being built.

The counterargument is the Jevons paradox and that cheaper intelligence will lead to more consumption of intelligence. I suspect that's true, but it's a question of magnitude. If AI becomes 1,000 times more computationally efficient, we need 1,000 times more equivalent workloads just to keep the existing infrastructure busy.

I think this is increasingly what the market is wrestling with. It's not necessarily questioning the potential of AI but rather how many chips, data centres and power plants will ultimately be needed, and how much of the debt incurred to build them will go bad.

I suspect many of the power plants still get built. Electricity is a commodity with plenty of alternative uses and a useful life measured in decades and governments now see the value in excess capacity. I'm considerably less certain about the economics of filling warehouses with specialized chips that could be rendered obsolete by a hyper-efficient models.

The trouble is that it's very difficult to draw a line around the losses. There are semiconductor companies, equipment manufacturers, data centre developers, private credit funds, utilities and a growing ecosystem of companies whose valuations are predicated on the capital intensity of artificial intelligence.

Moreover, we don't need an outright decline in demand for computing power for this to become a problem. We simply need demand to grow considerably more slowly than the infrastructure being built to accommodate it.

The great irony is that the most bullish possible outcome for artificial intelligence — that it becomes capable of rapid recursive self-improvement — may also be one of the most dangerous outcomes for the companies financing its physical infrastructure.

We're racing to build the railways at precisely the moment we are inventing the airplane.

-------------------------

item.title: What is order flow trading? How to read buying and selling pressure beyond chart patterns
item.description:
Why good chart patterns fail: What traders should know about market context and order flow

Heavy selling does not always mean prices are about to fall. Understanding how the market responds to buying and selling can help traders become more selective about their entries.

You learn a chart pattern, recognise it on your screen and enter a trade. A few minutes later, the market moves against you. You followed the textbook, so what went wrong?

Perhaps the pattern itself wasn't the problem. It was the market environment in which you decided to trade it.

In his Bookmap webinar, Understanding Market Context and Order Flow with Bruce, trader Bruce explains why understanding the bigger picture and observing the behaviour of buyers and sellers can be so valuable.

Understanding Market Context and Order Flow with Bruce. Source: Bookmap. Watch on YouTube.

Think of the market as an auction

Every completed trade involves a buyer and a seller. Yet some participants are more eager to trade than others.

Imagine a stock trading around $100.

Some buyers are happy to place limit orders at $99 and wait. Others want to buy immediately and are willing to accept the available selling price.

The first group provides liquidity by placing resting orders. The second takes liquidity by trading against available sell orders. In order flow terminology, we refer to these as passive and aggressive participants.

Traditional candlestick charts show where prices have traded. Order flow tools such as Bookmap allow traders to explore additional information, including executed trading volume and changes in resting liquidity within the available market data.

That distinction opens up some interesting possibilities for market analysis.

Same selling volume, two very different outcomes

Here is a simple example from investingLive to help you understand one of the more interesting aspects of order flow.

Imagine gold futures approaching an area of potential support at $2,600. Consider two hypothetical scenarios over comparable periods.

How effective is the selling?

Scenario A: Sellers are making progress

Aggressive sell volume: 100 contracts

Starting price: $2,600

Ending price: $2,598

Aggressive sellers execute 100 contracts. Available buy orders are consumed, and gold falls through $2,600 to $2,598.

Observation: The selling is producing meaningful downside movement, and potential support has been breached.

Scenario B: Sellers are struggling to make progress

Aggressive sell volume: 100 contracts

Starting price: $2,600

Ending price: $2,600

Aggressive sellers also execute 100 contracts, but this time those transactions repeatedly take place at $2,600. Sufficient passive buy orders are available to absorb the selling, and price does not break below the level.

Observation: Despite the same amount of aggressive selling, potential support holds during the observed period.

The lesson: The amount of aggressive selling is identical. Its effectiveness is not.

In the second hypothetical scenario, we are witnessing an example of absorption. Sellers are actively executing against buy orders, but they are unable to push prices lower during the observed period.

Does that mean you should immediately buy gold? Not necessarily.

The available buying liquidity could eventually be exhausted or withdrawn. Selling could then resume with greater effectiveness.

However, if aggressive buyers subsequently enter the market and prices begin moving higher, the potential reversal becomes more interesting.

Get into the habit of asking yourself not only how much buying or selling is taking place, but also what that activity is actually achieving.

Four things to consider before entering a trade

Bruce presents a useful process for approaching the market. Notice that finding an entry comes last.

1. Understand what is driving the market

Has an inflation report just been released? Is the Federal Reserve about to announce an interest rate decision? Has a major company reported earnings?

Understanding the circumstances surrounding a price move can help you anticipate changes in volatility and prepare for different outcomes.

2. Identify meaningful price levels

Start with previous daily and weekly highs and lows, overnight trading ranges and major round numbers.

You don't necessarily need twenty indicators on your chart. A handful of meaningful price levels can provide plenty of context.

3. Prepare for different scenarios

What would you expect to see if price reaches one of those levels? How would you recognise that support is holding? What would convince you that your original interpretation was wrong?

4. Look for your entry

Once you understand the context, location and possible scenarios, start looking for your trading setup.

Before entering, decide where your idea becomes invalid, how much you are prepared to risk and whether the potential reward justifies that risk.

What does a potential reversal look like in order flow?

One of the reversal setups discussed in Bruce's webinar brings together four observations:

  • Absorption of aggressive selling by passive buyers.
  • This activity occurs around a meaningful price level.
  • Price stops making lower lows and begins breaking above recent highs or a descending trend line.
  • Aggressive buyers help move prices higher.

The combination can provide more convincing evidence of a potential reversal than a familiar candlestick pattern alone.

How these elements develop will vary depending on the market environment. They should not be treated as a rigid formula that guarantees a successful trade.

Sometimes the absence of sellers is worth watching

Absorption is not the only behaviour traders can learn to recognise.

Imagine gold rallying strongly before gradually pulling back on relatively light volume.

A trader looking only at price might worry that the rally is ending. Order flow may reveal that aggressive selling during the pullback is relatively subdued.

This could be an early indication of selling exhaustion rather than significant new selling pressure.

If aggressive buying subsequently returns and price starts recovering, there may be a case for the original uptrend to continue.

If selling instead intensifies and price starts breaking through support, that interpretation needs to change.

The distinction is worth learning:

  • Absorption: Aggressive orders are met by sufficient passive liquidity, limiting price movement in the direction of those aggressive orders.
  • Exhaustion: Aggressive trading activity in one direction diminishes, suggesting that the pressure driving the move may be weakening.

Both can help explain why a market is struggling to move further in a particular direction, but neither guarantees what happens next.

Learning when not to trade

Markets spend considerable time moving sideways. Buyers push prices higher, sellers push them lower, and neither side establishes meaningful control.

These environments can be particularly frustrating when you are learning to trade. Almost every small price movement can look like the beginning of a bigger opportunity.

Sometimes the most sensible response is to wait.

Even when your market analysis is correct, chasing a move too late can leave you with an unattractive entry and excessive risk relative to the remaining potential reward.

There is no requirement to trade every time you sit in front of your charts.

A practical order flow exercise to try

If you have access to market replay, try the following exercise before risking real money.

The investingLive market replay exercise

  1. Open a historical trading session and mark the previous day's high and low.
  2. Watch what happens when price approaches either level.
  3. Observe whether aggressive buying or selling is increasing and whether that activity is producing further price movement.
  4. Look for possible absorption by comparing executed transactions with available resting liquidity.
  5. Pause the replay before the outcome becomes obvious. Write down your interpretation and what would convince you that it was wrong.
  6. Resume the replay and compare the outcome with your expectations.
  7. Repeat the exercise across ten different trading sessions, including trending and sideways markets.

Tip: Save examples where your interpretation was correct, but pay just as much attention to those where it failed.

Ten sessions will not establish whether you have a profitable trading strategy. They can, however, help you develop better observation habits and start building your own trading playbook.

Also remember that the order flow data you see depends on the instrument, exchange and data feed. A decentralised market such as spot forex does not have a single global order book.

One of the more valuable habits you can develop as a trader is learning to distinguish between market activity and its effectiveness.

Buyers and sellers can be very active without achieving much price progress. Understanding why is a good starting point for learning order flow.

For a deeper understanding of these concepts, watch Bruce's full Bookmap webinar on market context and order flow.

Educational only. Trade at your own risk.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold is sitting on the edge of support at $3,425 despite lower yields
item.description:
Gold is trading near $3,441, down about $115 or 3.24%, after reaching a low of $3,426.72. That low came in just above the bottom of a swing area on the daily chart between $3,425 and $3,500. The sellers took the price right to the edge. Can they get through it?

Stocks are getting hit, and gold is getting caught up in the selling

Lower yields would typically help gold. Gold pays no interest, so as Treasury yields move lower, the opportunity cost of holding it falls. Today, the liquidation across markets is taking precedence.

The Nasdaq Composite is down 4.10%, the S&P 500 is down 2.80%, and the Dow is down 1.70% in the snapshot above. When stocks are getting hit that hard, traders raising cash can sell what they own across markets. Gold is getting caught up in that selling today, even as yields move lower.

The $3,425 level defines the risk

For buyers looking for a bounce, the bottom of the swing area gives them a level to lean against with close risk. As long as the price holds above $3,425, they can stay in the game. A break below that level that stays below would give the sellers the go-ahead to probe lower, with the 61.8% retracement at $3,140.67 the next major downside target on the daily chart.

On the topside, the first job for buyers is to get and stay above $3,500. That would put the price back above the swing area and give buyers a technical victory. The next hurdle is the 50% midpoint at $3,610.01. Getting above both levels would do more to dig gold out of its bearish bias.

In the video, I show why the $3,425–$3,500 swing area matters, where buyers can define their risk, and what the price needs to do to give either side more control.

The education. Separate the reason from the risk.

Lower yields can give you a reason to look for a bounce in gold. The chart gives you a place to define your risk. Here, a trader leaning against $3,425 has a nearby level to judge whether the trade is working. If the price breaks and stays below it, the technical reason for leaning against support is gone. If it holds, watch how the price behaves at $3,500. That next test can tell you whether buyers are starting to take back some control.

item.title: This is the most-exciting moment in mathematics since Isaac Newton
item.description:
In the 17th century, Isaac Newton discovered calculus and changed the course of human civilization.

Until then, mathematics was poorly equipped to deal with a world that was constantly changing. Calculus gave us a systematic way to describe motion, acceleration, the accumulation of quantities and the relationships between them. It was an entirely new way of doing math.

It's difficult to overstate what that meant for humanity. Calculus became the foundation of modern physics and engineering. There is a straight line from that discovery to everything from the industrial revolution to putting a man on the moon.

I wonder if we're living through another one of those moments right now.

Last Friday, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge announced that, working with Claude, he had found a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. It's a problem that had stood since 1859 and is widely considered the most famous unsolved problem in mathematics. Two independent mathematical organizations have since expressed confidence in the proof.

That would have been enough to make 2026 a historic year in mathematics, but here's what's happened since.

Yesterday, OpenAI released nine mathematical papers with purported breakthroughs in:- Matrix multiplication- The computational complexity of Fourier transforms- Integer multiplication- The separation of VP and VNP- The sunflower conjecture- Strongly polynomial linear programming (Smale's ninth problem)

Then this morning, Google released another six papers produced by its AI research agent running on Gemini 4. They include breakthroughs in integer factorization, discrete logarithms, game theory, graph theory and computational complexity.

Now I don't understand what any of this means for math directly but I know a breakthrough when I see one.

Is it not obvious what's happening here?

These aren't obscure corners of mathematics. They're problems that have occupied some of the smartest people on the planet for decades.

Super intelligence has arrived in mathematics and it's coming for everything else. This is the proof you were waiting for.

This week I wrote that independent researchers at METR found evidence that AI development at Anthropic was already accelerating, with AI itself likely contributing to that acceleration. What we're seeing in mathematics offers a glimpse of how much further that process could go.

item.title: October new home sales 701k vs 650k
item.description:
• Prior was 676K (revised to 614K)

The US Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development publish the New Residential Sales report monthly at 10 am ET, usually in the last week of the month. It tracks sales of newly built single-family homes and is reported as a seasonally adjusted annualized rate.

Unlike existing home sales, which count closings, new home sales are recorded when a contract is signed or a deposit is accepted. That makes the report a more timely gauge of housing demand, reflecting buyers' decisions in the reference month rather than one or two months earlier. New homes account for only about 10% to 15% of total home sales, but they matter more for the economy because each one drives construction activity, hiring and spending on materials and furnishings.

The data are notoriously volatile. Margins of error are wide, and monthly changes are often not statistically significant. Revisions to the prior three months can be large enough to reverse the initial signal, so economists lean on three-month averages and longer trends.

The report also includes the median and average sales price of new homes, inventory of homes for sale and months' supply at the current sales pace. Inventory is broken down by homes not yet started, under construction and completed. A rising stock of completed, unsold homes is a warning sign for builders, since those are the homes they're most eager to move. Results are split by region: Northeast, Midwest, South and West.

Builders have leaned heavily on incentives, including mortgage rate buydowns and price cuts, to offset high borrowing costs. That has kept new home prices competitive with existing homes, where tight inventory and the lock-in effect have held prices up. The report rarely moves broader markets but is closely watched by homebuilder stocks.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin is following the stocks lower. What are the charts telling traders now?
item.description:
Bitcoin has been taking its cues from the US stock market this week. On Monday, the price spiked higher as stocks rebounded sharply following the reinstatement of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. On Tuesday, stocks gave back some of those gains as traders reassessed the rally, and Bitcoin followed them lower. Today, with the broader stock indices under more pressure, we are seeing follow-through selling in Bitcoin.

A snapshot of the major US indices shows the extent of the selling:

  • S&P 500 down 2.65%
  • Nasdaq Composite down 3.78%
  • Nasdaq 100 down 3.84%

The Trump administration’s tariff announcements are another headwind for risk sentiment. Inflation is already elevated, and companies facing higher import costs have a decision to make. They can absorb the extra costs and take a hit to margins, or they can try to pass them on to customers. If enough companies choose to protect their margins by raising prices, that could add to inflation pressure at a time when the Fed is trying to bring it down. For traders, that raises the question of how much room the Fed will have to ease if the economy starts to soften.

Sellers take out another swing area.

Technically, the first sign that Monday’s rebound was running out of steam came on Tuesday when Bitcoin moved back below the swing area between $61,183 and $62,470. Buyers had gotten above that area on Monday. Once the price fell back below it, sellers had an opening to push toward the next swing area between $57,735 and $58,035, which goes back to June and early July.

Today, the sellers pushed through that area, taking the price down to $57,209. That puts the focus on what happens on a bounce. Can the sellers keep the price below $57,735? If they can, the short-term bias remains to the downside. A move back into the area would take some of the pressure off, and a sustained move above $58,035 would give buyers a reason to probe higher. The $61,183–$62,470 area would still be a bigger hurdle on a more extended rebound.

On the downside, the next key target is the weekend low at $55,081, the lowest level going back to September 2024. A break below that level would put the focus on two downside targets from 2024 at $52,546 and then $49,607.

Education. Let the retest define the risk.

When the price breaks below a swing area, the first bounce can tell you more about who is in control. In this case, $57,735–$58,035 was an area where buyers had stepped in before. If the price bounces and sellers show up there, the old support is starting to act as resistance. That gives sellers a nearby area to lean against and a clear place to reassess if the price gets back above it.

The same area helps buyers frame their risk. A move above $58,035 that holds on a pullback would be a sign that buyers are starting to take back some control. If the price quickly falls through the area again, the buyers who acted on the break have a reason to reconsider. The weekend low at $55,081 is the downside target. The action around $57,735–$58,035 is what helps traders define the risk of looking for that move

item.title: As US stocks continue to fall, the flow of funds is leaning into the relative safety of the CHF.
item.description:
Monday’s rebound could not break the ceiling

The USDCHF moved higher on Monday as stocks rebounded, but the buyers could not get above the recent highs near 0.8443. That kept the ceiling in place. Yesterday, the price turned lower and broke below both the 100- and 200-hour moving averages as the stock gains started to unwind. Those breaks gave the sellers the go-ahead to start unwinding the November rally in the USDCHF as well.

Sellers extend the move lower

The selling continued today, with the price breaking below the swing area between 0.83395 and 0.83480 and slipping through a trend line on the hourly chart. The move then took out the 38.2% retracement at 0.83224 and the swing level at 0.8312.

That 0.8312 level is now the close-risk barometer for sellers. Stay below it, and the sellers remain more in control. Get and stay above it, and the buyers have an opening for a correction back toward 0.83224 and then the broken swing area at 0.83395–0.83480.

The 50% midpoint is the next test

The tumble has brought the pair down toward 0.8285, the 50% midpoint of the move up from the November low. If sellers can get and stay below that level, the next target is the swing area between 0.82636 and 0.82740. A break below that area would have traders looking toward the 61.8% retracement at 0.82478.

Trading education. A target and a risk level serve different purposes.

The 50% midpoint at 0.8285 is the downside target. The broken swing level at 0.8312 is where sellers can define their risk. If the price bounces and stalls below 0.8312, sellers have a level to lean against and can keep looking for a move through the midpoint. If the price gets and stays above 0.8312, the immediate bearish bias weakens and the focus shifts to how far the correction can go.

The same thinking applies at 0.8285. A quick move below the midpoint that reverses back above it tells you sellers had a shot and failed to follow through. If the price breaks below and then stalls against 0.8285 on a retest from underneath, the old target becomes a new level sellers can lean against. The next target is the swing area at 0.82636–0.82740.

In the video above, I walk through how Monday’s failed test of the ceiling set up yesterday’s moving-average breaks, why 0.8312 is the level sellers can lean against now, and what a break below 0.8285 would open up on the downside.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: US GDP 2nd Estimate for the 3rd quarter 4.3% vs 3.5 estimate
item.description:
The US GDP 2nd revision for the 3rd quarter is showing: 

  • Real GDP: 4.3% annualized vs 3.5% expected. Advance estimate 3.4%.
  • Consumer spending: 4.2% vs 3.8% previously reported.
  • GDP deflator: 1.8% vs 2.3% expected. Previously 2.2%.
  • Core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) prices: 2.5% vs 2.5% expected. Previously 2.5%.
  • Headline PCE prices: 2.1%, unchanged from the advance estimate.

The second estimate puts US third-quarter growth at a 4.3% annualized pace, well above the 3.5% Reuters consensus. The Bureau of Economic Analysis reported 3.4% in its advance estimate, making this a 0.9 percentage point upward revision. U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)

Household spending was stronger than first reported, with growth revised up to 4.2% from 3.8%. The inflation figures were more subdued. The GDP deflator came in below expectations at 1.8%, while core PCE inflation held at 2.5%, in line with forecasts.

What drove the upward revision to Q3 GDP?

US real GDP growth was revised up to 4.3% annualized from 3.4% in the advance estimate. Investment accounted for the largest upward revision, followed by consumer spending. Government spending added a little more, while exports and imports were slightly smaller drags.

The chart shows the following contributions to annualized GDP growth, in approximate percentage points:

  • Investment: +3.7 vs +3.3 in the advance estimate, the largest upward revision among the components.
  • Consumer spending: +2.8 vs +2.5, the second-largest upward revision.
  • Government spending: +1.0 vs +0.9, a modestly larger contribution.
  • Exports: −0.6 vs −0.7, a slightly smaller drag.
  • Imports: −2.6 vs −2.7, still the largest drag. Imports are subtracted in the GDP calculation.

Investment and consumer spending explain most of the 0.9 percentage point upgrade. Trade still weighed on growth, but a little less than first estimated.

Q3 price pressures eased. Core PCE was unchanged from the advance estimate.

The Bureau of Economic Analysis revised the gross domestic purchases price index down to 2.7% from 3.0% in the advance estimate. That was a sharp slowdown from 5.6% in Q2. All figures are seasonally adjusted annual rates. www.bea.gov

  • Headline PCE prices rose 2.1%, unchanged from the advance estimate and down from 5.0% in Q2. www.bea.gov
  • Core PCE prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 2.5%, unchanged from the advance estimate and down from 3.3% in Q2. www.bea.gov

For the Fed, the takeaway is that growth was revised higher while the quarterly core inflation reading held steady. The broader prices paid by US households, businesses and governments rose less than initially estimated, and headline consumer inflation slowed more sharply than core inflation from Q2.

Quick analysis

The growth surprise could give the Fed more room to lean toward a rate hike but the data is older. The market is still pricing in a near 100% chance of a 25 bp hike in December.  The data would normally lend support to the dollar and Treasury yields. The softer GDP deflator tempers that signal. Core PCE, the closer read on underlying consumer inflation, was unchanged from the advance estimate.

What this report measures

Real gross domestic product (GDP) measures the value of goods and services produced in the US after adjusting for inflation. The annualized rate shows how fast the economy would grow over a year if the quarter’s pace continued. The second estimate incorporates more complete data, and traders watch revisions to growth and inflation for clues about Fed policy.

The US stock is continuing to show sharp declines with the Nasdaq 100 down -764 points. The S&P is down -135 points and the Dow is down -633 points.  

The USD is showing a continued move into the CHF (USDCHF is lower), but is bouncing off the 50% midpoint at 0.8285.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: US Initial jobless claims 189K vs 200K estimate. Continuing claim 1.697M vs 1.721M estimate
item.description:
The weekly initial and continuing claims shows: 

  • Initial jobless claims (week ending November 21) — 189,000 vs 201,000 expected, down 13,000. Prior revised to 202,000 from 203,000. Forecast from Investing.com. investing.com
  • Four-week average of initial claims — 196,000, down 1,500. Prior revised to 197,500 from 197,750.

  • Continuing claims (week ending November 14) — 1,697,000, down 95,000. Prior revised to 1,792,000 from 1,763,000.
  • Four-week average of continuing claims — 1,724,750, up 500. Prior revised to 1,724,250 from 1,717,000.

  • Insured unemployment rate (week ending November 14) — 1.1%, down 0.1 percentage point. Prior revised to 1.2% from 1.1%.

The U.S. Department of Labor reported that initial jobless claims fell to 189,000 in the week ending November 21, below the 201,000 forecast. The four-week average also moved lower, pointing to fewer new filings over the past month. Continuing claims fell by 95,000 after the prior week was revised up by 29,000. Their four-week average edged higher despite the sharp weekly drop. U.S. Department of Labor

In the state data for the week ending November 14, Michigan posted the largest increase in initial claims (+6,036), while Missouri (−3,286) and New Jersey (−2,717) led the declines. New Jersey had the highest insured unemployment rate at 2.1% in the week ending November 7, followed by Washington at 2.0%.

Quick analysis

The downside surprise in initial claims points to limited layoff pressure and gives the Fed more reason to lean toward hikes. The market is pricing in a hike in December,and a 59% chance for a hike in January. That would normally lend some support to the US dollar and short-term Treasury yields.

What this report measures

Initial claims count new filings for unemployment insurance, while continuing claims count people who are still claiming benefits and are reported with an extra week’s lag. The national headline figures are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. Traders watch the four-week averages to smooth weekly swings and gauge whether the labor market is weakening.

item.title: US October PCE core inflation +0.3% m/m vs +0.3% expected
item.description:
Highlights of the Fed's personal consumption expenditure report for October 2026

  • Prior m/m +0.3%
  • Core PCE +3.3% y/y vs +3.2% expected
  • Prior was 3.1% y/y
  • Headline PCE +3.8% y/y vs +3.8% expected (prior 3.6%)
  • Deflator m/m +0.3% vs +0.3% expected (prior +0.5%)

Consumer spending and income for October:

  • Personal income +0.7% vs +0.4% expected. Prior month +0.2%
  • Personal spending +0.3% vs +0.4% expected. Prior month +0.5%
  • Real personal spending +0.0% vs 0.0% prior

There are no big surprises here, though the market could have done without the slightly hot core year-over-year number.

Last month I said we'd need another month to see if inflation was broadening. October doesn't settle that, but it doesn't make the worry go away either. Back-to-back core readings of 0.3% and 0.3% aren't consistent with getting anywhere near 2%. The more interesting part of the report is the consumer. Income beat by a wide margin, but spending fell short and real spending was flat for a second straight month. BEA says government benefits were boosted by one-time Medicare Improvement Fund premium rebates so that's likely the story. Most indications from retailers in reports from the past two weeks suggest that the US consumer is fine, in any case.

Digging into the data core goods inflation was about +0.4% m/m in October, the hottest since February (+0.7%). It was +0.2% in September and around 0.1% in the summer. The three-month annualized pace is about 2.7%, against about 1.6% over six months, so it's speeding up. That's an area the Fed has flagged as a concern.

Other nondurable goods rose 0.9%, its biggest gain since at least January 2025. That alone added about 8bp to core. Notably, 'recreational items' were the biggest driver of that, which is a sector that's particularly tariff-exposted. Magazines and newspapers were somehow also a large contributor, in defiance of a major secular slowdown.

This week, the Fed's Williams tilted more towards forward-looking inflation forecasts and away from the recent dogma of 'we have to get inflation to 2% first'. I suspect that's where the entire debate heads if oil and fuel prices continue to go down. I wouldn't say that with a tonne of confidence though as Warsh has tied himself to getting to target and 3.8% on headline is a long ways away.

I also worry that we're headed into annual price resets in many goods and companies are going to try to push through price hikes rather than eating them. 

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US October durable goods orders +0.2% vs +0.6% expected
item.description:
• Prior was 1.9%
  • Ex-transport +0.5% vs +0.5% expected
  • Prior ex-transport +0.5%
  • Ex-defense +0.4% vs +2.3% prior
  • Non-defense capital goods orders ex-air +1.2% vs +0.7% expected
  • Prior +0.6%

US durable goods orders continued to expand in October, giving another positive signal for the manufacturing sector. New orders for manufactured durable goods increased by $0.8 billion, or 0.2%, to $346.7 billion, following September's stronger 2.0% increase.

The headline increase was relatively modest, but the underlying details were more encouraging. Excluding transportation, new orders rose 0.5%, while orders excluding defense increased 0.4%. This suggests that the expansion was not solely driven by volatile transportation or defence-related demand.

Machinery was the main contributor to the monthly increase, with orders rising by $0.8 billion, or 1.8%, to $46.8 billion. The category has now increased in 21 of the past 22 months, highlighting the persistence of demand for industrial equipment and machinery.

Overall, durable goods orders have increased in seven of the past eight months, showing that demand for long-lasting manufactured products remains relatively resilient.

Keep in mind that the Durable Goods Orders report is almost never a market-moving release because it's very volatile and because it doesn't change anything for the Fed. Moreover, there's a positive correlation with the US Manufacturing PMI which releases much earlier. 

In fact, the Manufacturing PMI measures changes in manufacturing activity through business surveys. Its New Orders component is useful for assessing incoming demand and future production. So, by the time the Durable Goods data is released, the market has already factored in most of the economic expectations.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: US tariff details are better than the worst-case scenario implied yesterday
item.description:
The US is taking another step towards rebuilding the tariff regime that was struck down by the Supreme Court in February.

Yesterday's WSJ report highlighted the potential for broad new tariffs but the details from senior US officials in a Reuters report just out are somewhat better than feared.

  • Proposed 20% tariff on China, consistent with the existing trade agreement

  • New tariffs won't stack on top of the 10% and 12.5% forced-labor tariffs

  • Tariffs capped at 15% for South Korea, Taiwan, EU, Japan, Switzerland

  • Capped at 18% for Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Bangladesh

  • Capped at 20% for China

  • Implementation in January at the earliest

  • Final tariffs will be consistent with existing trade deals

  • More targeted tariffs on countries other than China

  • No new tariffs proposed on Mexico or Norway

  • US officials don't anticipate Chinese retaliation

  • Brazil faces additional tariffs under a separate Section 301 investigation, including a proposed 10% tariff on finished aircraft.

The biggest detail here is that the tariffs won't stack. That's effectively a 7.5 percentage point increase for China on goods currently subject to the 12.5% levy, something that was floated as far back as August.

Officials said China would warrant a 40% tariff in the absence of a trade agreement.

None of this should come as a big surprise. USTR Greer telegraphed on Friday that the industrial overcapacity investigation was nearing its conclusion and the administration has long signalled its intention to restore tariffs to previously negotiated levels.

The market has had plenty of time to digest that but there was some risk of a fresh escalation. On the whole, these details should come as a relief for most countries. I'd argue that Brazil is the one that's a problem, and Embraer in particular. Brazilian aircraft have enjoyed an exemption from US tariffs since February 24, when the previous 10% tariff was eliminated.

The US explicitly cited a lack of progress on digital trade and other issues as justification for the additional tariffs and you can't help but think the election results were a big part of this response.

The 14 economies identified for tariff action in the industrial overcapacity investigation are:

  • Bangladesh

  • Cambodia

  • China

  • European Union

  • India

  • Indonesia

  • Japan

  • South Korea

  • Malaysia

  • Singapore

  • Switzerland

  • Taiwan

  • Thailand

  • Vietnam

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.description:
Indian rupee has been on a sustained uptrend as oil prices kept falling steadily amid lower demand expectations on increased global growth concerns.

India is heavily dependent on imported crude, meaning higher oil prices require Indian importers to buy more dollars to pay for energy, increasing demand for USD and worsening the country's trade and current-account position. The reverse is true when oil prices fall.

Oil prices will likely continue to be the main driver but if growth concerns intensify further and markets go into heavy risk-off mode, we could see the rupee selling off on safe haven flows into US dollar.

In the big picture, the Indian Rupee remains on a bearish structural trend against the US dollar, so dip-buyers will continue to look for opportunities around strong major technical levels to keep pushing the USD/INR pair into new highs.

item.title: Solana's bearish outlook persists amid Fed tightening, prolonged US-Iran stalemate and growth concerns
item.description:
As most other cryptocurrencies, Solana spiked to the upside on Monday after the news of Jensen Huang being reinstated as Nvidia CEO triggered a strong rally in equity markets and helped improve the risk sentiment.

The gains were quickly faded, though, as the Nvidia news didn’t change the bigger picture and the underlying macro headwinds.

Moreover, the WSJ reported yesterday that the US is preparing to raise tariffs on China and other countries as early as this week.

As a reminder, following the Supreme Court ruling against the reciprocal tariffs, the Trump administration has been attempting to recreate a similar tariff structure through a different legal route, with country-specific investigations providing the justification.

This basically means that the Supreme Court ruling might have temporarily disrupted the tariff agenda without producing a lasting reduction in the effective tariff burden. So, we are going back to broadly similar levels to those imposed in 2025. Overall, this isn't a major gamechanger, but it still adds to inflation and growth concerns.

Keep in mind that the Fed is still expected to raise interest rates, with the extent of further tightening depending on incoming economic data and stock market conditions. Higher interest rates and tighter financial conditions remain a headwind for risk assets, especially cryptocurrencies like Solana, which are particularly sensitive to changes in liquidity and risk sentiment.

Meanwhile, the US-Iran stalemate remains unresolved, with Trump continuing to signal the possibility of renewed military action if negotiations fail. This keeps geopolitical risks elevated and adds another layer of uncertainty.

Therefore, the macro backdrop remains negative for Solana. Looking ahead, Solana will likely remain under pressure. A sustained recovery will likely need a more dovish Fed or a concrete breakthrough in US-Iran negotiations that improves growth expectations and the broader risk appetite.

 

SOLANA TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

item.title: Wall Street braces for another beatdown as US futures tumble, tech selloff deepens
item.description:
So much for a Thanksgiving comeback story this week, eh?

It's starting to get ugly out there again as the selling in US futures is intensifying ahead of the Wall Street open later today. S&P 500 futures are now down 1.7% while Nasdaq futures are down a whopping 2.6%. And a quick glance at the pre-market action tells you exactly where the pain is concentrated:

  • Nvidia (NVDA) -4.9%
  • AMD (AMD) -6.0%
  • Microsoft (MSFT) -2.5%
  • Tesla (TSLA) -2.6%
  • Amazon (AMZN) -3.5%
  • Alphabet (GOOGL) -3.2%

Ouch.

Nvidia is already poised to erase more than 10% of its stunning bounce from Monday while AMD is set to open at its lowest level since May. That kind of puts into perspective just how much of the enthusiasm surrounding the AI trade is being unwound.

And again, the most telling thing about the selloff in the past two days is just how quickly dip buyers have surrendered Monday's rather spectacular rebound. That is arguably the most concerning part in my view.

For all the excitement surrounding Jensen Huang's return, it seems that investors are back to asking the painful question about AI valuations and whether the spending frenzy can deliver the returns that markets have priced in. As mentioned earlier in the week:

"Markets love a good comeback story but one spectacular day doesn't undo several weeks of selling. The question now is can dip buyers build on yesterday's gains without another blockbuster headline to help them along. Until they make a more convincing case on the charts, there's still every chance that this will turn out as being another classic dead cat bounce. Don't get me wrong. I love me some good euphoria and there's a lot of dip-buying opportunities across multiple markets right now. However, let's not go too far to think that Jensen Huang returning is the formula to fix the intense scrutiny on lab ARR."

And when the biggest names on Wall Street are all getting hammered at the same time, there's only so much that the rest of the market can do to cushion the blow.

Besides that, just be mindful of the timing of things here. With Thanksgiving tomorrow and a shortened trading session on Friday, liquidity is likely to become thinner. And that can make for some rather exaggerated price swings, especially if investors are rushing to cut their exposure before the holiday period.

All eyes are on Wall Street again today and the big test for broader markets will be whether US stocks can absorb the selling pressure at the cash open or whether we see another wave of liquidation as the session progresses.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: What Are Barriers in Trading? Learn About Defined-Risk Contracts in Our Free Webinar
item.description:
Financial markets can move sharply in response to economic news, political developments and unexpected events. For retail traders, sudden price movements can result in significant losses, particularly when stop-loss orders are affected by market volatility and slippage.

Barriers offer an alternative approach to managing trading risk, allowing investors to define their maximum potential loss before opening a position.

Available to investors in the EEA, these derivative contracts include predefined barrier and take-profit levels, providing greater certainty over potential losses and trade execution.

But how do Barriers work, and what makes them different from traditional leveraged trading?

What Are Barriers in Trading?

Barriers are derivative contracts that allow traders to set predefined price levels at which their positions automatically close.

Traders pay an upfront premium, which represents their maximum potential loss. Unlike traditional margin-based trading, Barriers do not involve margin calls or negative balances under their stated terms.

Key features include:

  • Guaranteed stop-loss and take-profit: Positions close at the specified price when either level is reached.

  • Known risk: The upfront premium represents the maximum potential loss.

  • No margin calls: No additional margin is required.

  • Flexible expiry: Choose contract durations ranging from 30 minutes to 12 months.

  • Pattern trading: Use technical analysis to set barrier and take-profit levels.

  • AI pattern scanner: Identify potential chart patterns as they form.

These features offer traders another way to approach market opportunities while knowing their maximum potential loss upfront.

Who Should Consider Trading Barriers?

Barriers may interest experienced investors who want greater control over their trading risk and predefined exit levels.

They may be particularly relevant to traders who use technical analysis, follow chart patterns or want to explore alternatives to traditional margin-based products.

However, Barriers are complex derivative financial instruments and may not be suitable for everyone. If the market touches the barrier level, the contract ends and the entire premium is lost.

item.description:
Crude oil has been consolidating around the 80.00 handle as the selling pressure eased recently. Growth concerns could still push oil price lower, but we will likely need a bigger selloff in the stock market, an even more hawkish Fed or weak economic data to keep the bearish momentum going.

On the news front, Trump said that the Iran war was funded through January and that ending the Islamic Republic was probably achievable, although it was not his objective. Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Minister Katz warned that Iranian cells were operating inside the US with the intention of targeting senior officials, including Trump and his family, and claimed Iran was developing a dirty bomb.

Meanwhile, the military activity intensified around the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Iran's Navy claimed to have struck a container ship in the south of the Strait of Hormuz and said two tankers subsequently caught fire while travelling along unauthorised routes.

Overall, there’s been no de-escalation nor improvement in the US-Iran situation as the risk of a direct military confrontation remains high. Oil prices might remain under pressure if growth concerns intensify, but an escalation in the war could still push prices higher.

item.title: Ethereum remains under pressure as macro headwinds outweigh Nvidia-driven optimism
item.description:
Ethereum spiked to the upside on Monday as the news of Jensen Huang being reinstated as Nvidia CEO triggered a strong rally in equity markets and helped improve the risk sentiment in the crypto market too.

The move offered some relief after the heavy selling pressure seen towards the end of last week, but it didn't really change the bigger picture and as a result, the gains were eventually faded as the market refocused on the underlying macro headwinds.

Moreover, the WSJ reportedyesterday that the US is preparing to raise tariffs on China and other countries as early as this week.

As a reminder, after the Supreme Court ruling against the reciprocal tariffs, the Trump administration has been attempting to recreate a similar tariff structure through a different legal route, with country-specific investigations providing the justification.

This basically means that the Supreme Court ruling might have temporarily disrupted the tariff agenda without producing a lasting reduction in the effective tariff burden. So, we are going back to broadly similar levels to those imposed in 2025.

According to the Financial Times, the US is expected to honour previous trade agreements by capping the new tariffs for countries that had negotiated deals with the Trump administration. Overall, this isn’t a major gamechanger, but it still adds to inflation and growth concerns.

Keep in mind that the Fed is still expected to raise interest rates, with the extent of further tightening depending on incoming economic data and stock market conditions. Higher interest rates and tighter financial conditions remain a headwind for risk assets, especially cryptocurrencies, which are sensitive to changes in liquidity and risk appetite.

Meanwhile, the US-Iran stalemate remains unresolved, with Trump continuing to signal the possibility of renewed military action if negotiations fail. This keeps geopolitical risks elevated and adds another layer on uncertainty.

Therefore, the macro backdrop remains unfavourable for Ethereum and the crypto market in general. Looking ahead, Ethereum will likely remain skewed to the downside as long as macro conditions remain unchanged. A sustained recovery will likely require a more dovish Fed or a meaningful breakthrough in US-Iran situation that improves growth expectations.

 

ETHEREUM TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that Ethereumspiked into the resistance zone around the 1,870 level and eventually gave back all the gains as the sellers stepped in to position for a drop back into the 1,500 level. If the price gets there, we can expect the buyers to step in, with a defined risk below the 1,500 level, to position for a rally back into the 1,870 resistance. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower to increase the bearish bets into the 1,000 level next.
